usage: the all-purpose 존댓말 thanks to anyone
반말, to a close friend or someone younger
격식, public, written, or to a customer
examples: 감사합니다.
Thank you.
the bare safe thanks you can say to anyone
도와주셔서 감사합니다.
Thank you for helping me.
use ~아/어 주셔서 + 감사합니다 to thank for an action
바쁘신데 시간 내 주셔서 정말 감사합니다.
Thank you so much for making time despite being busy.
a full polite thank-you after someone goes out of their way
nuance: 감사합니다 is the default 존댓말 'thank you' you can say to literally anyone — a stranger, a clerk, a teacher, your boss — and never be wrong. It comes from Sino-Korean 감사(感謝). To go down in formality, switch to 고마워요 (still polite, warmer) or plain 고마워 (반말, only for friends and people clearly younger/closer); to go UP toward 격식, use 대단히 감사합니다 or 감사드립니다 in speeches and writing. The nearest alternative is 고맙습니다, which is pure native Korean and feels a touch warmer; the dividing line is mostly tone, not rank — both are equally polite. The classic English-speaker mistake is to thank for a noun with the wrong glue: you cannot say '도움 감사합니다' as if stacking words; to thank for an action you attach ~아/어 주셔서 (도와주셔서 감사합니다). Another is over-using 고마워 with strangers, which sounds rude.

mistakes: Saying 고마워 to a stranger, clerk, or anyone older — that is 반말 and sounds rude; default to 감사합니다 or at least 고마워요.
Trying to thank for an action by just naming it ('도와 감사합니다') — Korean needs ~아/어 주셔서: 도와주셔서 감사합니다.
Writing 감사 합니다 with a space — 감사합니다 is one word; the space is wrong.

usage: 반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
softer polite, to a peer or familiar adult
examples: 고맙습니다.
Thank you.
the warm native-Korean polite thanks
챙겨 줘서 고마워.
Thanks for looking out for me.
반말 with ~아/어 줘서 between close friends
이렇게까지 신경 써 주셔서 고맙습니다.
Thank you for going to all this trouble for me.
heartfelt thanks when someone did more than expected
nuance: 고맙습니다 is the native-Korean twin of 감사합니다 and is equally polite — many Koreans feel it sounds a little warmer and more personal, while 감사합니다 feels slightly more formal/standard. You say it to anyone in 존댓말; drop to 고마워요 (gently polite) or 고마워 (반말) as closeness rises and age/rank falls. The dividing line versus 감사합니다 is feel and origin (native vs Sino-Korean), NOT politeness level — never think 고맙습니다 is 'less polite'. English speakers stumble on the verb stem: the dictionary form is 고맙다, so the polite ending is 고맙습니다 (with ㅂ), and the 반말 is 고마워 (the ㅂ becomes 워), never 'goma' or '고맙어'. Another pitfall is reaching only for 감사합니다 in every situation; sprinkling 고맙습니다 to people you know sounds more human.

Saying 고마워요 to your boss in a formal setting — prefer 고맙습니다 or 감사합니다; 고마워요 can feel a touch too casual upward.

usage: polite reply to thanks; slightly formal/old-fashioned
반말, brushing off a friend's thanks
the natural everyday reply people actually use
examples: 천만에요.
You're welcome.
the textbook reply to 감사합니다
고마워요. — 천만에요, 도움이 됐다니 다행이에요.
Thank you. — You're welcome, I'm glad it helped.
softening 천만에요 with a follow-up so it isn't stiff
덕분에 잘 끝냈어요. — 천만에요, 별것도 아닌데요.
Thanks to you it went well. — You're welcome, it was really nothing.
pairing with 별것 아니에요 for a humble, natural close
nuance: 천만에요 is the dictionary answer to 'thank you', but in real life it sounds a little formal or even old-fashioned, so Koreans more often say 아니에요, 별말씀을요, or 별거 아니에요 to wave off thanks. The literal sense is '(that's) ten million [words]', i.e. 'far from it, not at all'. Register: 천만에요 is polite; the 반말 brush-off is 뭘 or 아니야; the most 격식 form is 천만의 말씀입니다. The dividing line versus 별말씀을요 is that 별말씀을요 is gentler and more humble (used when a senior or customer thanks you), while 천만에요 can feel slightly textbook. The English-speaker mistake is treating 천만에요 like the constant, reflexive 'you're welcome' of English; Koreans often answer thanks with 네 + a smile or 아니에요, and over-firing 천만에요 sounds stilted.

Saying 천만에요 to a close friend — too formal; use 뭘 or 아니야 in 반말.
Misspelling it 천만애요 — it is 천만에요 (에, not 애).

english: Don't mention it. / Not at all.
usage: humble polite reply, often upward to a senior/customer
반말-ish casual shortening among close people
you're too kind to say so (formal)
격식, very humble deflection of praise/thanks
examples: 별말씀을요.
Don't mention it.
humble reply when someone thanks or praises you
덕분에 큰 도움 받았습니다. — 별말씀을요.
You were a huge help. — Please, don't mention it.
deflecting a senior's thanks modestly
바쁘신데 직접 와 주셔서 감사합니다. — 별말씀을요, 당연히 와야죠.
Thank you for coming in person. — Not at all, of course I'd come.
pairing with 당연히 ~죠 to sound gracious
nuance: 별말씀을요 is a humble, polite way to wave off thanks OR praise, literally '(what) unusual words (you say)' — i.e. 'you needn't say such a thing'. It is the go-to when someone above you (a customer, a senior, an elder) thanks you and you want to sound modest, softer than 천만에요. Register: polite/humble by default; the 격식 expansion is 별말씀을 다 하십니다; casually you might hear a clipped 별말을. The dividing line versus 천만에요 is humility and direction — 별말씀을요 leans 'I'm too humble to accept this thanks' and works beautifully upward, while 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook. English speakers mis-segment it: the 말씀 is the honorific word for 'words/speech', and the ending is 을요 (often written 별말씀을요), not '별 말씀 이요'. Also, do not use it to a close friend — it is too formal; say 뭘 instead.

Breaking it into 별 말씀 with a space or writing 별말씀이요 — the set phrase is 별말씀을요.
Thinking it only answers thanks — it also gracefully deflects praise ('you flatter me').

usage: the safe 존댓말 apology to anyone, esp. seniors/strangers
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
examples: 죄송합니다.
I'm sorry.
the bare polite apology, safe with anyone
늦어서 죄송합니다.
I'm sorry I'm late.
use ~아/어서 + 죄송합니다 to apologize for a reason
제 실수로 불편을 드려서 정말 죄송합니다.
I'm truly sorry for the inconvenience my mistake caused.
a full apology owning the fault in a formal situation
nuance: 죄송합니다 is the higher-courtesy 'I'm sorry', from Sino-Korean 죄송(罪悚), literally 'I feel I've committed a fault/I'm fearful before you'. Because it carries that deferential nuance, it is the apology you give to strangers, seniors, customers, and your boss. The 반말 partner is 미안해 (from 미안하다), used downward/among close friends; the gentler polite form is 미안해요; the 격식 upgrade is 대단히 죄송합니다 or 죄송스럽습니다. The dividing line versus 미안하다 is deference: 죄송하다 lowers yourself and is safer upward, while 미안하다 is more horizontal and personal. The English-speaker mistakes: (1) attaching the reason wrong — to apologize for doing X you use X-아/어서 죄송합니다 (늦어서 죄송합니다), not '늦은 것 죄송'; (2) using 미안해 to a boss, which is far too casual; (3) confusing it with 실례합니다, which is 'excuse me' for a small intrusion, not a real apology.

Forming the reason wrong, e.g. '늦은 거 죄송' — use the ~아/어서 connector: 늦어서 죄송합니다.
Swapping in 실례합니다 to apologize for a real mistake — 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor intrusion, not an apology for fault.

usage: 존댓말 to a peer or familiar adult; warm, personal
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, neutral and a bit firmer
natural extension adding sincerity in 반말
examples: 미안해요.
I'm sorry.
a soft, personal polite apology to someone close-ish
연락 늦어서 미안해.
Sorry for the late reply.
everyday 반말 apology with ~아/어서 to a friend
내가 약속을 못 지켰네. 정말 미안해.
I couldn't keep my promise. I'm really sorry.
owning a let-down to a friend, warmer than 죄송
nuance: 미안해요/미안하다 is the warmer, more horizontal 'sorry' — used downward or sideways: to friends, peers, your kids, people younger or close to you. From 미안(未安), literally 'not at ease (in my heart)'. The ladder is 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gently polite) → 미안합니다 (firmer polite) → 죄송합니다 (deferential, upward/格式). The key dividing line versus 죄송하다: 미안하다 does NOT lower you, so it can feel too casual or even slightly presumptuous toward a senior or customer — for them choose 죄송합니다. English speakers wrongly treat 미안해요 and 죄송해요 as interchangeable 'sorry'; using 미안해요 to your boss sounds under-deferential, while using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds oddly stiff and distant. Also note: a quick 'sorry, excuse me' to squeeze past a stranger is NOT 미안해요 but 실례합니다 / 잠시만요.

Using 미안하다 to brush past someone in a crowd — Koreans say 실례합니다 or 잠시만요, not 미안해요, for that.
Saying 미안해 to someone you've just met — too familiar; with strangers use 미안합니다/죄송합니다.

english: It's okay. / That's all right. / No, thank you.
usage: polite; reassuring, accepting an apology, or politely declining
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, firmer and more neutral
yes, it's fine / no, I'm okay
natural extension; context tells accept vs decline
examples: 괜찮아요.
It's okay.
the all-purpose reassurance / soft refusal
죄송해요. — 괜찮아요, 그럴 수도 있죠.
I'm sorry. — It's okay, these things happen.
accepting an apology graciously
한 잔 더 드릴까요? — 아니요, 괜찮아요. 잘 마셨습니다.
Shall I pour you another? — No, I'm fine, thank you. I've had plenty.
괜찮아요 used to politely decline an offer
nuance: 괜찮아요 does triple duty: 'it's okay / don't worry about it' (accepting an apology), 'I'm fine' (about your state), and crucially 'no, thank you' (politely declining an offer). The decline meaning trips up English speakers most: when a host offers food or a refill and you say 괜찮아요, you are turning it DOWN, not accepting — so to accept you must say 네, 주세요, not 괜찮아요. Register: 괜찮아 (반말) → 괜찮아요 (polite) → 괜찮습니다 (firmer/격식). The nearest relatives are 됐어요 (also 'I'm good/no need', but can sound curt) and 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing'); 괜찮아요 is the soft, safe choice. The standard mistake is hearing '괜찮아요?' as merely 'are you okay?' and missing that a flat 괜찮아요 to an offer means 'no thanks' — leaving learners unfed at Korean tables.

usage: 존댓말 to get attention, pass by, or interrupt a stranger
clipped/반말-ish, only among close people or muttered
격식, before entering or doing something intrusive
natural extension; 저 softens the approach
examples: 실례합니다.
Excuse me.
polite opener to a stranger before a question or to pass
실례합니다, 화장실이 어디예요?
Excuse me, where's the restroom?
use 실례합니다 + question to approach a stranger
실례합니다, 잠깐 지나가도 될까요?
Excuse me, may I squeeze past for a moment?
asking permission to pass in a tight space
nuance: 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor social intrusion — getting a stranger's attention, asking a question, passing by, or entering a space. From Sino-Korean 실례(失禮), literally 'I'm committing a breach of etiquette'. It is NOT an apology for a real fault (that's 죄송합니다) and NOT just 'sorry'. Register: 실례합니다 is polite; the 격식 form is 실례하겠습니다 / 실례하지만; you almost never say it in 반말 (a clipped 실례 sounds odd). The nearest alternatives are 저기요 and 잠시만요/잠깐만요: 저기요 hails a server or stranger casually, 잠시만요 means 'one moment / let me through', while 실례합니다 is the more polished, formal opener. English speakers misuse it as an all-purpose 'sorry' or 'pardon?' — to ask someone to repeat, you say 네? or 다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요?, not 실례합니다.

mistakes: Using 실례합니다 as 'sorry' for a real mistake — for fault use 죄송합니다; 실례합니다 is only for a small intrusion.
Saying 실례합니다 to mean 'pardon? / say again?' — to ask for a repeat use 네? or 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Hailing a waiter with 실례합니다 every time — Koreans more often call 저기요 or 여기요 in casual eateries.

english: Excuse me, but… / Pardon me, but…
usage: polite lead-in to a slightly intrusive question
pardon me, may I ask you something
격식, very polite preface to a question
excuse me, but might you happen to…
natural extension; 혹시 softens a personal question
examples: 실례지만, 누구세요?
Excuse me, but who are you?
softening a direct question with 실례지만
실례지만 나이가 어떻게 되세요?
Pardon me, but how old are you?
prefacing a sensitive personal question politely
실례지만 길 좀 여쭤봐도 될까요?
Excuse me, but may I ask you for directions?
a courteous full request to a stranger on the street
nuance: 실례지만 is the polite 'excuse me, but…' you put in FRONT of a question that might intrude — asking a stranger's name, age, whether a seat is taken, or for directions. It is 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but', i.e. 'it's rude of me, but…'. It softens nosy or imposing questions, especially personal ones, where Korean expects cushioning. Register: 실례지만 is polite; 실례하지만 and 실례합니다만 are slightly more 격식; a softer/casual variant is 실례인데. english: Thank you for your hard work. / Well done.
usage: thank you for your hard work
polite, to a peer/junior or sideways after work is done
반말, downward to someone younger or a close junior
격식, more respectful acknowledgment of effort
examples: 수고하셨습니다.
Thanks for your hard work.
standard sign-off after a shared task or shift
오늘 회의 수고하셨습니다. 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.
Thanks for your work in today's meeting. I'll head out first.
leaving the office after a meeting
늦게까지 작업하시느라 고생 많으셨습니다. 수고하셨어요.
You worked so hard until late. Great job.
warmly thanking a colleague for a long effort
nuance: 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges effort — 'you've worked hard, thank you' — said when a task, shift, meeting, or service is finished. It's the standard workplace sign-off and also what you say to a delivery driver or staff who just did something for you. To a superior, prefer 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 said carefully. Also, the present 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work') is for someone still working, while 수고하셨습니다 (past) is for when it's done — don't mix the tenses.

usage: polite; crediting someone for a good outcome
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, firmer and more neutral
examples: 덕분이에요.
It's thanks to you.
crediting the other person for how well things went
잘 지내셨어요? — 네, 덕분에 잘 지냈어요.
Have you been well? — Yes, thanks to you I've been well.
the set polite reply '덕분에 + (잘 …)'
이번 일 잘 끝났어요. 다 부장님 덕분입니다.
This project wrapped up well. It's all thanks to you, sir.
giving a senior full credit, modest and warm
nuance: 덕분 means 'thanks to (your) help/grace/virtue' (德分), so 덕분에 / 덕분이에요 credits another person for a good result — it's gratitude that says 'because of you, things went well'. It shines as a humble, gracious move toward someone who helped, especially a senior. The set phrase 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 is the warm standard reply to 'how have you been?'. Register: 덕분이야 (반말) → 덕분이에요/덕분에요 (polite) → 덕분입니다 (firmer/격식). The vital contrast English speakers miss is 덕분 vs 때문: 덕분 is for POSITIVE outcomes ('thanks to'), while 때문 is neutral-to-negative cause ('because of', often blame) — saying '너 때문에' to mean 'thanks to you' actually sounds like 'it's your fault'. So credit good things with 덕분에, never 때문에. Also, 덕분에 needs the result clause or stands as 덕분이에요; you can't use it as a bare noun reply like English 'thanks to you!' shouted alone without 이에요/에.

english: Thank you for your thoughtfulness / for caring.
usage: polite; thanking someone for taking trouble/care
thanks for caring / for the trouble
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식, to a customer/senior, written or spoken
thank you for going to such trouble
examples: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다.
Thank you for your thoughtfulness.
thanking someone who took extra care for you
몸은 좀 어떠세요? — 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다, 많이 좋아졌어요.
How are you feeling? — Thank you for asking/caring; I'm much better.
responding warmly to concern about your health
선물까지 챙겨 주시고, 이렇게 신경 써 주셔서 정말 감사합니다.
You even prepared a gift — thank you so much for all your thoughtfulness.
thanking someone who went out of their way for you
nuance: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 thanks someone for the care, attention, or trouble they took on your behalf — for worrying about you, asking after you, or quietly handling something. 신경(을) 쓰다 literally means 'to use one's nerves', i.e. 'to pay attention / take pains / fret over'. The polite engine is the favor pattern ~아/어 주셔서 ('because you kindly did…') + 감사합니다. Register: 신경 써 줘서 고마워 (반말) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 (polite) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다 (격식). The nearest alternative is the plainer 도와주셔서 감사합니다 ('thanks for helping'); the dividing line is that 신경 써 주셔서 specifically thanks for the emotional care/attention and effort, not just a concrete action. English-speaker mistakes: writing 신경써 with no space (it's 신경(을) 쓰다, so 신경 써), and using plain 신경 써서 (no 주다), which drops the gratitude-for-a-favor nuance and sounds like you're just describing that they worried.

english: Excuse me! (to get attention) / Over here!
usage: the everyday polite way to flag a stranger or call a server
calling staff to YOUR table; signaling your spot
반말-ish, soft opener to a friend or to trail into a question
we'd like to order over here
natural extension; flagging staff to take an order
examples: 저기요, 이거 얼마예요?
Excuse me, how much is this?
flagging a shop clerk to ask a question
여기요, 물 좀 주세요.
Excuse me (over here), some water please.
calling a server to your table in a restaurant
저기요, 이거 떨어뜨리셨어요.
Excuse me, you dropped this.
getting a passing stranger's attention to help them

Both are polite-but-casual: perfectly normal in shops, cafés, and restaurants, but they can feel a touch blunt toward a clear senior or in a formal setting, where 실례합니다 / 실례지만 is more polished. Register: bare 저기 is the soft 반말-ish opener to someone you know ('저기, 있잖아'); 저기요/여기요 add 요 for strangers and staff. The dividing line versus 실례합니다 is polish and intent: 저기요/여기요 simply get attention quickly and are the real-life default in eateries, while 실례합니다 is more formal and also covers passing by or interrupting. English speakers either over-use 실례합니다 everywhere (sounding stiff) or, worse, try to summon a waiter by saying 미안해요 or by snapping/saying nothing — in Korea you call out 저기요 or 여기요 clearly, which is normal and not rude.

english: I ask for your understanding. / Please bear with us.
usage: 격식 polite; announcements, notices, to customers
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
we ask that you kindly understand (very formal)
natural extension; 너른/넓은 양해 = generous understanding
examples: 양해 부탁드립니다.
We ask for your understanding.
closing line of an apology/notice for an inconvenience
공사로 인해 소음이 있을 수 있으니 양해 부탁드립니다.
There may be noise due to construction, so we ask for your understanding.
a typical posted/announced notice
배송이 다소 지연되고 있습니다. 고객님들의 너른 양해 부탁드립니다.
Shipping is somewhat delayed. We ask for our customers' kind understanding.
a business apologizing for a delay
nuance: 양해 부탁드립니다 is a formal, slightly stiff 'please understand / bear with us', used to ask people to tolerate an inconvenience — delays, noise, closures, policy. 양해(諒解) is Sino-Korean for 'understanding/making allowances'; 부탁드리다 is the humble 'I (respectfully) request'. This is announcement/customer-service language: signs, intercom notices, emails, formal apologies. Register: it is inherently 격식; the still-more-formal variant is 양해해 주시기 바랍니다; casually to a friend you'd shrink it to 양해 좀 해 줘 / 이해해 줘. The nearest everyday alternative is 이해해 주세요 ('please understand'), which is warmer and more personal; the dividing line is formality and audience — 양해 부탁드립니다 addresses a group/customers from an institution, 이해해 주세요 is one-to-one. English speakers misuse it in casual one-on-one chat (it sounds like a corporate announcement), and they mis-handle 부탁: it pairs with 드립니다/드려요 (humble) upward, not '부탁합니다' shouted at an equal as a demand.

english: Excuse me for a second. / Let me just slip in for a moment.
usage: polite; before passing, reaching past, or briefly intruding
반말-ish/clipped, among close people or muttered
please excuse me for a moment (formal)
격식, before stepping away or entering
just one quick second, excuse me
examples: 잠깐 실례할게요.
Excuse me for a second.
said as you reach past or step by someone
잠깐 실례할게요, 여기 좀 지나갈게요.
Excuse me a sec, let me get through here.
squeezing past in a tight aisle
통화 좀 하고 올게요. 잠시 실례하겠습니다.
I need to take a call. Please excuse me for a moment.
politely stepping away from a meeting
nuance: 잠깐 실례할게요 is 'excuse me for a moment' — a brief, courteous heads-up before you reach past someone, slip by, step away, or briefly intrude. 잠깐/잠시 = 'for a short while', 실례하다 = 'commit a small breach of etiquette', and ~ㄹ게요 announces YOUR own imminent action ('I'm going to…'). Register: clipped 잠깐 실례 (casual) → 잠깐 실례할게요 (polite) → 잠시 실례하겠습니다 (격식). The ~ㄹ게요 vs ~ㄹ겠습니다 split tracks formality. The nearest alternatives are 잠시만요 / 잠깐만요 ('one moment / let me through'), which are shorter and very common, and bare 실례합니다 (a touch more formal). The dividing line: 잠깐 실례할게요 explicitly flags a short, self-initiated intrusion politely, while 잠시만요 can also mean 'hold on / wait'. English-speaker mistakes: using ~ㄹ게요 toward a senior where ~겠습니다 is safer; and saying 잠깐 실례하세요 — the 하세요 form orders the OTHER person to excuse themselves, but you mean YOURSELF, so it must be 실례할게요/실례하겠습니다.

english: Are you okay? / Is everything all right?
usage: 존댓말; checking on someone who stumbled, looks unwell, etc.
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식, e.g. staff to a customer or a senior
natural extension; 혹시 softens the check-in
examples: 괜찮으세요?
Are you okay?
checking on someone right after a stumble or shock
어, 괜찮으세요? 많이 놀라셨죠.
Oh, are you okay? That must have startled you.
showing concern after someone bumps or trips
안색이 안 좋아 보이는데, 괜찮으세요? 좀 쉬실래요?
You look pale — are you all right? Want to rest a bit?
a caring full check-in on someone unwell
nuance: 괜찮으세요? is the polite 'are you okay?' — the honorific question form of 괜찮다, used to check on someone who tripped, got startled, looks unwell, or had a hard time. It's a small but vital courtesy: when you bump someone or they stumble, Koreans immediately ask 괜찮으세요?, often with 죄송합니다. The nearest alternative is 어디 안 좋으세요? ('is something wrong / are you unwell?'), which specifically asks about feeling sick; 괜찮으세요? is broader. English-speaker mistakes: dropping the honorific and asking 괜찮아? to a stranger or senior (too casual); and confusing the statement 괜찮아요 ('I'm fine / no thanks') with the question 괜찮으세요? — intonation and the 으세요 ending mark the question, and they are NOT interchangeable.

(반말) → 괜찮으세요? (polite) → 괜찮으십니까? (격식). It's a small but vital courtesy: when you bump someone or they stumble, Koreans immediately ask 괜찮으세요?, often with 죄송합니다.
The nearest alternative is 어디 안 좋으세요? ('is something wrong / are you unwell?'), which specifically asks about feeling sick; 괜찮으세요? is broader.
The honorific infix 으시 + polite 어요 gives 괜찮으세요?, raising the LISTENER.

Saying 괜찮해요/괜찮하세요 — there's no ㅎ; the stem is 괜찮다 → 괜찮아요, 괜찮으세요.

english: I'd like to ask a favor. / Please (I'm counting on you).
usage: humble polite; making a request of a senior/customer
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
I look forward to working with you / please take care of this
격식, first meetings, handing off a task
may I ask you a small favor
examples: 부탁드립니다.
I'm counting on you, please.
closing a request humbly and politely
이 자료 검토 좀 부탁드립니다.
Could I ask you to review this document, please?
asking a colleague/senior for a task with 부탁드립니다
처음 뵙겠습니다. 앞으로 잘 부탁드립니다.
Nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.
the set first-meeting line in work/social life
nuance: 부탁드립니다 is the humble, polite way to ASK a favor or entrust a task — 부탁(을) 하다 ('to make a request') raised to the humble 부탁(을) 드리다 ('to (respectfully) offer a request upward'). The set phrase 잘 부탁드립니다 is indispensable: it greases first meetings ('please be good to me / I look forward to working with you') and task hand-offs ('please take care of this'). Register: 부탁해 (반말) → 부탁해요 (polite) → 부탁드립니다 (humble/격식). The dividing line versus a bare imperative like 해 주세요 ('please do it') is deference and softness: 부탁드립니다 frames the whole thing as a humble plea, far gentler than a direct command, which Korean prefers upward. English-speaker mistakes: using the plain 부탁합니다 or 부탁해 toward a senior (use the humble 부탁드립니다); and treating 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'please do it well' — it's a fixed social formula of goodwill, not a comment on quality.
